title: Dopamine D2-receptor blockade in humans disrupts the effect of effort on learning
experiments_summary: A double-blind, randomized, between-subjects pharmacological study was conducted in 42 healthy adults (placebo n=19, sulpiride n=23). Participants received either a single 800mg oral dose of sulpiride (a D2-receptor antagonist) or placebo and waited 2 hours before task onset. Physiological measures (heart rate, blood pressure) and subjective state (Bond and Lader Visual Analogue Scales) were recorded at baseline and hourly. Blinding integrity was assessed using the Bang Blinding Index. Motor capacity was assessed via maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) calibration using hand-held dynamometers (BIOPAC SS25LA), with target force levels standardized as proportions of MVC (low=5%, high=44%). Participants completed a two-armed bandit reward learning task (2 blocks of 150 trials each) in which they selected between two abstract stimuli by exerting pre-specified low or high physical force, receiving probabilistic binary feedback. Stimulus-reward contingencies changed every 12 or 24 trials without signaling. Behavioral analyses included ANOVAs on choice accuracy, win-stay, and lose-switch behavior as a function of drug group and stimulus effort level, with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons and Greenhouse-Geisser sphericity corrections. Computational modeling compared three reinforcement learning models (M1: standard Rescorla-Wagner; M2: dual learning rates for positive/negative outcomes; M3: effort-modulated learning rate asymmetry) fit via maximum likelihood estimation and compared using AIC and Akaike weights. Model identifiability and parameter reliability were assessed via model recovery analyses (100 simulations per model, 20 agents each). Permutation tests (1,000 iterations) verified that effort-sensitive learning rates and parameter correlations were not artifacts of model fitting. Simulation analyses tested the adaptive role of effort-learning coupling by generating four groups of n=100 agents varying in effort aversion (k) and learning rate asymmetry (phi), analyzed with two-way between-subjects ANOVAs on simulated choice accuracy.
